messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (average voltage in 0.7-0.8s window).
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (maximum voltage over 0-0.8s).
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.02\text{V}$ (peak-to-peak ripple in 0.7-0.8s window).
        *   $T_{up} \le 0.15\text{s}$ (time to reach 1.8V).
        *   $dV \le 0.01\text{V}$ (stability between 0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s windows).
    *   Piezo: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30nF) and $20\text{M}\Omega$ leakage.
    *   Open-circuit voltage: $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$ (at S1).

    *   FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) fails on:
        *   $V_{pp}$ (ripple is too high: $26.2\text{mV}$ at S1 vs $20\text{mV}$ limit).
        *   $T_{up}$ (startup is too slow: $0.269\text{s}$ vs $0.15\text{s}$ limit).
        *   $V_{out\_min}$ (at S2 and S4, it doesn't reach 1.8V).
        *   $V_{out\_max}$ (at S3, it exceeds 3.6V: $5.72\text{V}$).
        *   $dV$ (stability).
    *   The FBR is basically just a diode bridge and a capacitor. The output is $V_{out} \approx V_{oc} - 2V_d$. With $V_{oc}=3.2\text{V}$ and $V_d=0.25\text{V}$, $V_{out} \approx 2.7\text{V}$. However, the energy extraction is inefficient because it only charges when $V_{piezo} > V_{out} + 2V_d$.

    *   *Problem 1: Efficiency/Startup/Min Voltage.* To improve energy extraction from a piezo (which is a capacitive source), we need to invert the charge. Standard SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) or SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction) are good.
    *   *Problem 2: Maximum Voltage.* A Zener clamp (DZ33) can limit $V_{out}$ to 3.3V, satisfying $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{V}$.
    *   *Problem 3: Ripple.* A larger storage capacitor $C_{out}$ reduces ripple, but might slow down startup. However, $2.2\mu\text{F}$ was used in the reference. We might need more or a better regulation method.
    *   *Problem 4: Startup Time.* This is the hardest part. Fast startup requires high power delivery early on.

    *   **Topology A: SSHI-like (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor)**.
        *   Use an inductor and a switch to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks.
        *   Circuit: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Bridge $\rightarrow$ Storage.- Wait, a simpler version is the "Parallel-SSHI".
        *   Let's try a basic SSHI: Piezo in parallel with a switch and inductor that shorts $C_p$ at the peaks to flip the voltage. But we need to get that energy to the output.
        *   Better: A buck-boost or a charge-pump. But the constraints on components (16) and the nature of the source suggest a synchronized rectifier or a SECE-like circuit.

    *   **Topology B: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)**.
        *   The piezo charges an inductor/capacitor during the half-cycle, and then dumps it to the output at the peak.
        *   Simple SECE: Piezo $\rightarrow$ $L$ $\rightarrow$ Switch $\rightarrow$ Storage. This is more complex.

    *   **Topology C: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge)**.
        *   Replacing diodes with switches. But we only have 2 SYNC controllers and 4 switches. A full bridge requires 4 switches. If we have 2 SYNCs, we can do 2 switches.

    *   **Topology D: Half-Bridge / Charge Pump**.
        *   Using an inductor to step up the voltage or invert the piezo capacitance.
        *   Structure: Piezo $\rightarrow$ L $\rightarrow$ Switch $\rightarrow$ Diode $\rightarrow$ Out.

    *   *Design 1: SSHI (Inductive Inversion).*
        *   Piezo terminals: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   A switch $S_1$ and inductor $L_1$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   When $S_1$ closes, $L_1$ and $C_p$ exchange energy, flipping the voltage across $C_p$.
        *   Wait, if $S_1$ and $L_1$ are just in parallel, they don't move energy to `out`.
        *   We need a rectifier.
        *   Proposed connectivity:
            1.  Piezo $\rightarrow$ Full Bridge (DSCH) $\rightarrow$ `out`.
            2.  Parallel to piezo: $S_1$ and $L_1$.
            3.  $S_1$ closes at peaks (edges: both) to flip $V_{Cp}$.
            4.  This increases the voltage across the bridge, improving $V_{avg}$ and $T_{up}$.
            5.  Add Zener (DZ33) to `out` for $V_{max}$.
            6.  Large $C_{out}$ for ripple.

    *   *Design 2: SECE-lite.*
        *   Piezo $\rightarrow$ $L_1$ $\rightarrow$ $S_1$ $\rightarrow$ $D_1$ $\rightarrow$ `out`.
        *   This isn't standard. Let's try a different approach.

    *   *Design 3: Buck-Boost / Charge-Pump based on SYNC.*
        *   Let's try a simpler "Inductor-assisted rectifier".
        *   Piezo $\rightarrow$ $L_1$ $\rightarrow$ $S_1$ (SYNC) $\rightarrow$ $D_1$ $\rightarrow$ `out`.
        *   Actually, the most robust simple harvester for these specs is often the SSHI.

    *   *Refining Design 1 (SSHI):*
        *   Diodes: $D_1$ (`pzp`, `out`), $D_2$ (`pzn`, `out`), $D_3$ (`0`, `pzp`), $D_4$ (`0`, `pzn`). (Wait, full bridge: $D_1$: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`, $D_2$: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out` is not a bridge. Correct bridge: $D_1$: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`, $D_2$: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out` is wrong. Let's use the standard one provided in the prompt's example: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`).
        *   Actually, the provided example for the full bridge is: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`. Let's check the current:
            *   $V_{pzp} > V_{out} \implies D_1$ conducts.
            *   $V_{pzn} > V_{out} \implies D_2$ conducts.
            *   $V_{pzp} < 0 \implies D_3$ conducts.
            *   $V_{pzn} < 0 \implies D_4$ conducts.
            *   This is a standard bridge if the piezo is symmetric about 0.
        *   Now, the inversion: Switch $S_1$ and $L_1$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   $S_1$ nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`. $L_1$ nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   Wait, if $S_1$ and $L_1$ are in parallel, they just short the piezo. We need $L_1$ in series with $S_1$.
        *   $S_1$ nodes: `pzp`, `n1`. $L_1$ nodes: `n1`, `pzn`.
        *   $S_1$ ctrl: `G1`. `G1` edges: `both`. `ton` $\approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        *   $C_{out}$ on `out`.
        *   Zener $D_Z$ on `out`.

    *   *Refining Design 2 (Modified SSHI - only one side):*
        *   Instead of a full bridge, use a half-bridge to reduce diode drops (better for S4/S2).
        *   Piezo `pzn` to `0`.
        *   `pzp` $\rightarrow$ $D_1$ $\rightarrow$ `out`.
        *   Inversion: $L_1$ and $S_1$ between `pzp` and `0`.
        *   This only works for half the cycle.

    *   *Refining Design 3 (Symmetric SSHI with Zener):*
        *   Full bridge (DSCH)
        *   $L_1$ and $S_1$ in parallel with the piezo (`pzp` to `pzn`).
        *   $C_{out}$ (large)
        *   $D_{zener}$ (DZ33) to cap `out` at 3.3V.
        *   Let's try a very large $C_{out}$ to kill the ripple.

    *   S1: $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{V}$, $R_L = 330\text{k}\Omega$. $P_{load} \approx 1.8^2/330\text{k} \approx 10\mu\text{W}$.
    *   S2: $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$. $P_{load} \approx 1.8^2/150\text{k} \approx 21.6\mu\text{W}$. (Heavy load!)
    *   S3: $R_L = 2200\text{k}\Omega$. $P_{load} \approx 1.8^2/2.2\text{M} \approx 1.5\mu\text{W}$. (Strong excitation!)
    *   S4: $I_p = 30\mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 1000\text{k}\Omega$. $P_{load} \approx 1.8^2/1\text{M} \approx 3.2\mu\text{W}$. (Weak excitation!)
    *   S5: $f = 80\text{Hz}$.
    *   S6: $C_p = 30\text{nF}$.

    *   For SSHI, $L$ is typically in the mH range. For $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $L=10\text{mH} \implies \pi \sqrt{L C} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-2} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 15.7\mu\text{s}$.

    *   Topology 1: Full-Bridge + SSHI (Inductor-Switch parallel to piezo) + Zener + $C_{out}$.
    *   Topology 2: Half-Bridge + SSHI (Inductor-Switch parallel to piezo) + Zener + $C_{out}$. (Less diode drop, but only half the energy). Let's stick to full bridge for S2/S4.
    *   Topology 3: Full-Bridge + $C_{out}$ + Zener (Basically the FBR but with Zener and better $C_{out}$ tuning). No, FBR already failed, we need the inversion to get more power for S2 and S4.

    *   Let's reconsider the "Symmetric SSHI".
        *   $L_1$ and $S_1$ are in parallel with the piezo (`pzp` and `pzn`).
        *   When $S_1$ closes at the peak, $C_p$ discharges into $L_1$, then $L_1$ reverses the voltage on $C_p$.
        *   The bridge then extracts this "extra" voltage.

    *   Components:
        *   $D_1$: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out` (DSCH)
        *   $D_2$: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out` (DSCH)
        *   $D_3$: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp` (DSCH)
        *   $D_4$: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (DSCH)
        *   $L_1$: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `n1`
        *   $S_1$: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (ctrl: `G1`)
        *   $G_1$: `SYNC` (edges: `both`, phase: 0, ton: $20\mu\text{s}$)
        *   $C_1$: `out` $\rightarrow$ `0` (value: $10\mu\text{F}$)
        *   $D_z$: `0` $\rightarrow$ `out` (DZ33)

    *   Wait, let's double check the bridge again.
        *   `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp`
        *   `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
        *   If $V_{pzp} = 3\text{V}$ and $V_{pzn} = -3\text{V}$, $D_1$ conducts. If $V_{pzp} = -3\text{V}$ and $V_{pzn} = 3\text{V}$, $D_2$ conducts. $D_3$ and $D_4$ provide the return path to ground. Yes, that's a full bridge.

    *   What about the startup time? $T_{up} \le 0.15\text{s}$.
        $C_{out} = 10\mu\text{F}$ might be too large for a $0.15\text{s}$ startup. Let's try $2.2\mu\text{F}$ as in the reference, but the SSHI will provide more current.
        Actually, the $C_{out}$ value is optimized by the evolution strategy. I should provide a reasonable starting value.

    *   $L$ value: $10\text{mH}$ is a good start.
    *   $T_{on}$: $20\mu\text{s}$ is a good start.

    *   Is there a better way? SECE?
        *   SECE usually involves an inductor and a switch that connects the piezo to the output at the peak.
        *   Example: $L$ between `pzp` and `n1`, $S$ between `n1` and `out`.
        *   This is often more efficient than SSHI. Let's try one SECE-like structure.
        *   `pzp` $\rightarrow$ $L_1$ $\rightarrow$ $S_1$ $\rightarrow$ `out`. (Only works for one half cycle).
        *   To make it symmetric:
            *   $L_1$ between `pzp` and `n1`, $S_1$ between `n1` and `out`.
            *   $L_2$ between `pzn` and `n2`, $S_2$ between `n2` and `out`.
            *   $S_1$ closes at positive peak, $S_2$ at negative peak.
            *   This would use 2 SYNCs, 2 Switches, 2 Inductors.
            *   Let's see:
                *   $L_1$: `pzp`, `n1`
                *   $S_1$: `n1`, `out` (ctrl `G1`, edges `pos`)
                *   $L_2$: `pzn`, `n2`
                *   $S_2$: `n2`, `out` (ctrl `G2`, edges `neg`)
                *   $G_1$: `SYNC` (pos)
                *   $G_2$: `SYNC` (neg)
                *   $C_{out}$, $D_z$.
            *   This extracts energy from $C_p$ by transferring it to $L$ and then to `out`.
            *   Actually, a simpler SECE uses a capacitor to store the energy first. But we are limited to 16 components.

    *   Let's try the SSHI first, as it's more common.

    *   *Check on S3 (Strong Excitation):*
        $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$. The Zener $D_z$ (DZ33) is crucial here.

    *   *Check on S4 (Weak Excitation):*
        SSHI should help increase the voltage above the diode drops.

    *   *Check on Ripple:*
        $V_{pp} \le 0.02\text{V}$. This requires a reasonably large $C_{out}$. The evolution strategy will tune it.

    *   *Check on Startup:*
        $T_{up} \le 0.15\text{s}$. The inversion increases power, which should speed up startup.

    *   Wait, in the SSHI design:
        $L_1$ and $S_1$ in parallel with the piezo.
        $S_1$ closes at $V_{pzp}$ peaks.
        When $S_1$ closes, $C_p$ discharges into $L_1$. Then it reverses.
        This means the piezo voltage $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$ flips from $V_{peak}$ to $-V_{peak}$.
        This is a change of $2 V_{peak}$.
        The bridge then sees this and can charge $C_{out}$ more effectively.

    *   *Is the Zener enough for $V_{max}$?*
        $D_z$ (DZ33) has a breakdown at 3.3V. This should keep $V_{out} \le 3.6\text{V}$.

    *   Let's propose two designs:
        1. SSHI with Full Bridge.
        2. SSHI with Half Bridge (to see if the lower diode drop helps S2/S4). Actually, the prompt says the bridge is `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.

    *   Let's refine the SSHI connectivity.
        - `D1`: `pzp`, `out`
        - `D2`: `pzn`, `out`
        - `D3`: `0`, `pzp`
        - `D4`: `0`, `pzn`
        - `L1`: `pzp`, `n1`
        - `S1`: `n1`, `pzn`
        - `G1`: `SYNC`, edges `both`, ton `20u`, phase `0`
        - `C1`: `out`, `0`
        - `Dz`: `0`, `out` (DZ33)

    *   Wait, if the `S1` and `L1` are in parallel with the piezo, and it's a full bridge, the bridge will still be there during the inversion. Is that okay? Yes, because the inversion happens very fast ($20\mu\text{s}$), and the bridge diodes will either be blocked or conduct the inverted current.

    *   Wait, a better SSHI (Parallel-SSHI) often uses an extra capacitor and a switch to avoid the diode drops during the main phase. But that's more complex. Let's start with this.

    *   Let's consider another topology for Proposal 2: a "Charge Pump" or "Voltage Doubler" if possible.
        But the current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ is perfectly suited for SSHI.

    *   Actually, let's try a second variant of the SSHI with a different switch timing or a different bridge. No, just different connectivity.
        How about a "Half-Bridge SSHI" for Proposal 2?
        - `D1`: `pzp`, `out`
        - `D2`: `0`, `pzp` (wait, that's just a diode to ground)
        - Actually, a half-bridge is just `pzn` tied to `0`, and `pzp` $\rightarrow$ $D_1 \rightarrow$ `out`.
        - And `L1`, `S1` between `pzp` and `0`.
        - This only extracts half the energy but has fewer diode drops.

    *   Wait, there's another efficient one: the "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE).
        - $C_p$ charges a capacitor $C_{ext}$ through a diode.
        - At the peak, a switch $S_1$ connects $C_{ext}$ to `out`.
        - Connectivity:
            - $D_1$: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `n1`
            - $C_{ext}$: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `0`
            - $S_1$: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `out` (ctrl `G1`, edges `pos`)
            - $D_2$: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `n2`
            - $C_{ext2}$: `n2` $\rightarrow$ `0`
            - $S_2$: `n2` $\rightarrow$ `out` (ctrl `G2`, edges `neg`)
            - $C_{out}$, $D_z$.
        - This is very efficient. Let's try this as Proposal 2.

    *   Let's double-check the components:
        - Proposal 1: 4 Diodes (Bridge), 1 Inductor, 1 Switch, 1 Sync, 1 Capacitor, 1 Zener = 9 components.
        - Proposal 2: 2 Diodes, 2 Capacitors (ext), 2 Switches, 2 Syncs, 1 Capacitor (out), 1 Zener = 10 components.

    *   Let's check if the "Full Bridge" in the reference was using DSCH. Yes. DSCH drop is $\sim 0.25\text{V}$.
        $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{V}$. $V_{out} \approx 3.2 - 0.5 = 2.7\text{V}$.
        The problem in the reference was not the diode drop (which is small for DSCH) but the efficiency of extracting energy from $C_p$. SSHI and SECE solve this.

    *   Final polish of Proposal 1 (SSHI):
        - `D1`: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
        - `D2`: `pzn`, `out` (DSCH)
        - `D3`: `0`, `pzp` (DSCH)
        - `D4`: `0`, `pzn` (DSCH)
        - `L1`: `pzp`, `n1`
